minutes.headline: Committee voted down consultant's community-approval scoring, will review the master-plan matrix line by line itself
minutes.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed OverUnder's updated recommendation matrix and scoring methodology for the town's draft master plan, with several members objecting that the 'community approval summary' leaned too heavily on very small samples (a 4-person steering-committee survey and a 5-person engagement matrix) next to 187 public survey responses. After extensive debate over sample size, methodology, contract cost, and whether other town boards and commissions should get input, the committee voted down accepting the community approval summary as presented, then voted to have each member individually mark accept/reject with reasons on every strategy in the matrix and submit it to the staff liaison before the next meeting.

what_happened.line: Committee rejected the consultant's community-approval scoring, which had weighted a 4-person and a 5-person sample alongside 187 public survey responses.
Members voted instead to individually mark accept or reject, with reasons, on every strategy in the master-plan matrix themselves.
Formal reorganization of the committee was postponed again because some members' swearing-in status was unconfirmed.
A member flagged that most of the OverUnder consulting contract has already been paid out relative to what has been delivered.
Submissions must go to the staff liaison, Matt, rather than the chair, to avoid members discussing the matrix among themselves outside a meeting.

why_it_matters: The master plan sets the strategies the town will pursue on housing, zoning and land use, and this vote means each committee member's individual judgment -- not a consultant's scoring formula -- will decide what survives into the draft.

A resident who wants a strategy in or out of the plan should watch their own board or commission for a chance to weigh in, since several members raised whether bodies like the Agricultural Commission get a say before the plan is finalized.
The contract-cost concern touches how much of the town's money has already gone to outside consulting relative to what the plan currently contains.
